{{Short description|Conjugate transpose of an operator in infinite dimensions}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[operator theory]], each [[linear operator]] <math> A </math> on an [[inner product space]] defines a '''Hermitian adjoint''' (or '''adjoint''') operator <math>A^*</math> on that space according to the rule

:<math>\langle Ax,y \rangle = \langle x,A^*y \rangle,</math>

where <math>\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle</math> is the [[inner product]] on the [[vector space]].

The adjoint may also be called the '''Hermitian conjugate''' or simply the '''Hermitian'''<ref>{{Cite book |first=David A. B. |last=Miller |title=Quantum Mechanics for Scientists and Engineers |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=2008 |pages=262, 280}}</ref> after [[Charles Hermite]].  It is often denoted by {{math|''A''<sup>†</sup>}} in fields like [[physics]], especially when used in conjunction with [[bra–ket notation]] in [[quantum mechanics]].  In [[dimension (vector space)|finite dimensions]] where operators can be represented by [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]], the Hermitian adjoint is given by the [[conjugate transpose]] (also known as the Hermitian transpose).

The above definition of an adjoint operator extends verbatim to [[bounded operator|bounded linear operator]]s on [[Hilbert space]]s <math>H</math>.  The definition has been further extended to include unbounded ''[[Densely defined operator|densely defined]]'' operators, whose domain is topologically [[dense (topology)|dense]] in, but not necessarily equal to, <math>H.</math>

== Informal definition ==

Consider a [[linear map]] <math>A: H_1\to H_2</math> between [[Hilbert space]]s. Without taking care of any details, the adjoint operator is the (in most cases uniquely defined) linear operator <math>A^* : H_2 \to H_1</math> fulfilling 
:<math>\left\langle A h_1, h_2 \right\rangle_{H_2} = \left\langle h_1, A^* h_2 \right\rangle_{H_1},</math>

where <math>\langle\cdot, \cdot \rangle_{H_i}</math> is the [[Inner product space#Hilbert space|inner product]] in the Hilbert space <math>H_i</math>, which is linear in the first coordinate and [[conjugate linear]] in the second coordinate. Note the special case where both Hilbert spaces are identical and <math>A</math> is an operator on that Hilbert space.

When one trades the inner product for the [[Dual system#Canonical duality on a vector space|dual pairing]], one can define the adjoint, also called the [[Transpose of a linear map|transpose]], of an operator <math>A: E \to F</math>, where <math>E, F</math> are [[Banach spaces]] with corresponding [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]] <math>\|\cdot\|_E, \|\cdot\|_F</math>. Here (again not considering any technicalities), its adjoint operator is defined as <math>A^*: F^* \to E^*</math> with
:<math>A^*f = f \circ A : u \mapsto f(Au), </math>

i.e., <math>\left(A^*f\right)(u) = f(Au)</math> for <math>f \in F^*, u \in E</math>.

The above definition in the Hilbert space setting is really just an application of the Banach space case when one identifies a Hilbert space with its dual (via the [[Riesz representation theorem]]). Then it is only natural that we can also obtain the adjoint of an operator <math>A: H \to E</math>, where <math>H</math> is a Hilbert space and <math>E</math> is a Banach space. The dual is then defined as <math>A^*: E^* \to H</math> with <math>A^*f = h_f </math> such that 
:<math>\langle h_f, h\rangle_H = f(Ah).</math>

== Definition for unbounded operators between Banach spaces ==
{{move section from|Transpose of a linear map|section=yes|date=March 2026}}
Let <math>\left(E, \|\cdot\|_E\right), \left(F, \|\cdot\|_F\right)</math> be [[Banach space]]s. Suppose <math> A: D(A) \to F </math> and <math>D(A) \subset E</math>, and suppose that <math>A</math> is a (possibly unbounded) linear operator which is [[Densely defined operator|densely defined]] (i.e., <math>D(A)</math> is dense in <math>E</math>). Then its adjoint operator <math>A^*</math> is defined as follows. The domain is
:<math>D\left(A^*\right) := \left\{g \in F^*:~ \exists c \geq 0:~ \mbox{ for all } u \in D(A):~ |g(Au)| \leq c \cdot \|u\|_E\right\}.</math>

Now for arbitrary but fixed <math>g \in D(A^*)</math> we set <math>f: D(A) \to \R</math> with <math>f(u) = g(Au)</math>. By choice of <math>g</math> and definition of <math>D(A^*)</math>, f is (uniformly) continuous on <math>D(A)</math> as <math>|f(u)| = |g(Au)| \leq c\cdot \|u\|_E</math>. Then by the [[Hahn–Banach theorem]], or alternatively through extension by continuity, this yields an extension of <math>f</math>, called <math>\hat{f}</math>, defined on all of <math>E</math>. This technicality is necessary to later obtain <math>A^*</math> as an operator <math>D\left(A^*\right) \to E^*</math> instead of <math>D\left(A^*\right) \to (D(A))^*.</math> Remark also that this does not mean that <math>A</math> can be extended on all of <math>E</math> but the extension only worked for specific elements <math>g \in D\left(A^*\right)</math>.

Now, we can define the adjoint of <math>A</math> as
:<math>\begin{align}
  A^*: F^* \supset D(A^*) &\to E^* \\
                        g &\mapsto A^*g = \hat f.
\end{align}</math>

The fundamental defining identity is thus

:<math>g(Au) = \left(A^* g\right)(u)</math> for <math>u \in D(A).</math>

== Definition for bounded operators between Hilbert spaces ==<!-- This section is linked from [[Dipole]] -->
Suppose {{mvar|H}} is a complex [[Hilbert space]], with [[inner product]] <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle</math>. Consider a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] [[linear operator]] {{math|''A'' : ''H'' → ''H''}} (for linear operators, continuity is equivalent to being a [[bounded operator]]). Then the adjoint of {{mvar|A}} is the continuous linear operator {{math|''A''<sup>∗</sup> : ''H'' → ''H''}} satisfying

: <math>\langle Ax , y \rangle = \left\langle x , A^* y\right\rangle \quad \mbox{for all } x, y \in H.</math>

Existence and uniqueness of this operator follows from the [[Riesz representation theorem]].<ref name=rs186>{{harvnb|Reed|Simon|2003|pp=186–187}}; {{harvnb|Rudin|1991|loc=§12.9}}</ref>

This can be seen as a generalization of the ''adjoint'' matrix of a square matrix which has a similar property involving the standard complex inner product.

== Properties ==
The following properties of the Hermitian adjoint of [[bounded operator]]s are immediate:<ref name=rs186 />
# [[Involution (mathematics)|Involutivity]]: {{math|1=''A''<sup>∗∗</sup> = ''A''}}
# If {{mvar|A}} is invertible, then so is {{math|''A''<sup>∗</sup>}}, with <math display="inline">\left(A^*\right)^{-1} = \left(A^{-1}\right)^*</math>
# [[Antilinear map|Conjugate linearity]]:
#* {{math|1=(''A'' + ''B'')<sup>∗</sup> = ''A''<sup>∗</sup> + ''B''<sup>∗</sup>}}
#* {{math|1=(''λA'')<sup>∗</sup> = {{overline|''λ''}}''A''<sup>∗</sup>}}, where {{math|{{overline|''λ''}}}} denotes the [[complex conjugate]] of the [[complex number]] {{math|''λ''}}
# "[[Distributive property#Antidistributivity|Anti-distributivity]]": {{math|1=(''AB'')<sup>∗</sup> = ''B''<sup>∗</sup>''A''<sup>∗</sup>}}

If we define the [[operator norm]] of {{mvar|A}} by
:<math>\| A \|_\text{op} := \sup \left\{\|Ax\| : \|x\| \le 1\right\}</math>

then
:<math>\left\|A^* \right\|_\text{op} = \|A\|_\text{op}.</math><ref name=rs186 />

Moreover,
:<math>\left\|A^* A \right\|_\text{op} = \|A\|_\text{op}^2.</math><ref name=rs186 />

One says that a norm that satisfies this condition behaves like a "largest value", extrapolating from the case of self-adjoint operators.

The set of bounded linear operators on a complex Hilbert space {{mvar|H}} together with the adjoint operation and the operator norm form the prototype of a [[C*-algebra]].

== Adjoint of densely defined unbounded operators between Hilbert spaces ==
===Definition===
Let the inner product <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle</math> be linear in the ''first'' argument. A [[densely defined operator]] {{mvar|A}} from a complex Hilbert space {{mvar|H}} to itself is a linear operator whose domain {{math|''D''(''A'')}} is a dense [[linear subspace]] of {{mvar|H}} and whose values lie in {{mvar|H}}.<ref>See [[unbounded operator]] for details.</ref> By definition, the domain {{math|''D''(''A''<sup>∗</sup>)}} of its adjoint {{math|''A''<sup>∗</sup>}} is the set of all {{math|''y'' ∈ ''H''}} for which there is a {{math|''z'' ∈ ''H''}} satisfying
: <math> \langle Ax , y \rangle = \langle x , z \rangle \quad \mbox{for all } x \in D(A).</math>

Owing to the density of <math>D(A)</math> and [[Riesz representation theorem]], <math>z</math> is uniquely defined, and, by definition, <math>A^*y=z.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Reed|Simon|2003|p=252}}; {{harvnb|Rudin|1991|loc=§13.1}}</ref>

Properties 1.–5. hold with appropriate clauses about [[domain of a function|domains]] and [[codomain]]s.{{clarify|reason=These will be hard to guess.|date=May 2015}} For instance, the last property now states that {{math|(''AB'')<sup>∗</sup>}} is an extension of {{math|''B''<sup>∗</sup>''A''<sup>∗</sup>}} if {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}} and {{mvar|AB}} are densely defined operators.<ref>{{harvnb|Rudin|1991|loc=Thm 13.2}}</ref>

===ker A{{sup|*}} = (im A){{sup|⊥}}===
For every <math>y \in \ker A^*,</math> the linear functional <math>x \mapsto \langle Ax,y \rangle = \langle x,A^*y\rangle </math> is identically zero, and hence <math> y \in (\operatorname{im} A)^\perp.</math>

Conversely, the assumption that <math> y \in (\operatorname{im} A)^\perp</math> causes the functional <math>x \mapsto \langle Ax,y \rangle</math> to be identically zero. Since the functional is obviously bounded, the definition of <math>A^*</math> assures that <math> y \in D(A^*).</math> The fact that, for every <math> x \in D(A),</math> <math>\langle Ax,y \rangle = \langle x,A^*y\rangle = 0</math> shows that <math> A^* y \in D(A)^\perp =\overline{D(A)}^\perp = \{0\}, </math> given that <math>D(A)</math> is dense.

This property shows that <math>\operatorname{ker}A^*</math> is a topologically closed subspace even when <math>D(A^*)</math> is not.

===Geometric interpretation===
If <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math> are Hilbert spaces, then <math>H_1 \oplus H_2</math> is a Hilbert space with the inner product

:<math>\bigl \langle (a,b),(c,d) \bigr \rangle_{H_1 \oplus H_2} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \langle a,c \rangle_{H_1} + \langle b,d \rangle_{H_2}, </math>

where <math>a,c \in H_1</math> and <math>b,d \in H_2.</math>

Let <math>J\colon H\oplus H \to H \oplus H</math> be the [[symplectic matrix|symplectic mapping]], i.e. <math>J(\xi, \eta) = (-\eta, \xi).</math> Then the graph
:<math>G(A^*) =\{(x,y) \mid x\in D(A^*),\ y=A^*x\} \subseteq H \oplus H </math>
of <math> A^* </math> is the [[orthogonal complement]] of <math>JG(A):</math>
:<math>G(A^*) = (JG(A))^\perp = \{ (x, y) \in H \oplus H : \bigl \langle (x, y) , (-A\xi, \xi) \bigr \rangle_{H \oplus H} = 0\;\;\forall \xi \in D(A)\}. </math>

The assertion follows from the equivalences

:<math> \bigl \langle (x, y) , (-A\xi, \xi) \bigr \rangle = 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad  \langle A\xi, x \rangle = \langle \xi, y \rangle, </math>

and

:<math>\Bigl[ \forall \xi \in D(A)\ \ \langle A\xi, x \rangle = \langle \xi, y \rangle \Bigr]  \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad x \in D(A^*)\ \&\ y = A^*x. </math>

====Corollaries====
=====A{{sup|*}} is closed=====
An operator <math>A</math> is ''closed'' if the graph <math>G(A)</math> is topologically closed in <math>H \oplus H.</math> The graph <math>G(A^*)</math> of the adjoint operator <math>A^*</math> is the orthogonal complement of a subspace, and therefore is closed.

=====A{{sup|*}} is densely defined ⇔ A is closable=====
An operator <math>A</math> is ''closable'' if the topological closure <math>G^\text{cl}(A)  \subseteq H \oplus H </math> of the graph <math>G(A)</math> is the graph of a function. Since <math>G^\text{cl}(A)</math> is a (closed) linear subspace, the word "function" may be replaced with "linear operator". For the same reason, <math>A</math> is closable if and only if <math>(0,v) \notin G^\text{cl}(A)</math> unless <math>v=0.</math>

The adjoint <math> A^* </math> is densely defined if and only if <math>A</math> is closable. This follows from the fact that, for every <math>v \in H,</math>

:<math>v \in D(A^*)^\perp\ \Leftrightarrow\ (0,v) \in G^\text{cl}(A),</math>

which, in turn, is proven through the following chain of equivalencies:
:<math>
\begin{align}
v \in D(A^*)^\perp &\Longleftrightarrow (v,0) \in G(A^*)^\perp 
\Longleftrightarrow (v,0) \in (JG(A))^\text{cl} = JG^\text{cl}(A) \\
&\Longleftrightarrow (0,-v) = J^{-1}(v,0) \in G^\text{cl}(A) \\
&\Longleftrightarrow (0,v) \in G^\text{cl}(A).
\end{align}
</math>

=====A{{sup|**}} = A{{sup|cl}}=====
The ''closure'' <math> A^\text{cl} </math> of an operator <math>A</math> is the operator whose graph is <math> G^\text{cl}(A) </math> if this graph represents a function. As above, the word "function" may be replaced with "operator". Furthermore, <math> A^{**} = A^{\text{cl}},</math> meaning that <math> G(A^{**}) = G^{\text{cl}}(A). </math>

To prove this, observe that <math>J^* = -J,</math> i.e. <math> \langle Jx,y\rangle_{H \oplus H} = -\langle x,Jy\rangle_{H \oplus H},</math> for every <math>x,y \in H \oplus H.</math> Indeed,
:<math>
\begin{align}
\langle J(x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2)\rangle_{H \oplus H}
&= \langle (-x_2,x_1),(y_1,y_2)\rangle_{H \oplus H}
= \langle -x_2,y_1\rangle_H + \langle x_1,y_2 \rangle_H \\
&= \langle x_1,y_2 \rangle_H + \langle x_2,-y_1 \rangle_H
= \langle (x_1,x_2),-J(y_1,y_2)\rangle_{H \oplus H}.
\end{align}
</math>
In particular, for every <math>y \in H \oplus H</math> and every subspace <math> V \subseteq H \oplus H,</math> <math>y \in (JV)^\perp</math> if and only if <math>Jy \in V^\perp.</math> Thus, <math> J[(JV)^\perp] = V^\perp </math> and <math> [J[(JV)^\perp]]^\perp = V^\text{cl}.</math> Substituting <math> V = G(A),</math> obtain <math> G^\text{cl}(A) = G(A^{**}).</math>

=====A{{sup|*}} = (A{{sup|cl}}){{sup|*}}=====
For a closable operator <math>A,</math> <math> A^* = \left(A^\text{cl}\right)^*, </math> meaning that <math>G(A^*) = G\left(\left(A^\text{cl}\right)^*\right).</math> Indeed,
:<math>
G\left(\left(A^\text{cl}\right)^*\right) = \left(JG^\text{cl}(A)\right)^\perp = \left(\left(JG(A)\right)^\text{cl}\right)^\perp = (JG(A))^\perp = G(A^*).
</math>

===Counterexample where the adjoint is not densely defined===
Let <math>H=L^2(\mathbb{R},l),</math> where <math>l</math> is the linear measure. Select a measurable, bounded, non-identically zero function <math>f \notin L^2,</math> and pick <math>\varphi_0 \in L^2 \setminus \{0\}.</math> Define

:<math>A \varphi = \langle f,\varphi\rangle \varphi_0.</math>

It follows that <math>D(A) = \{\varphi \in L^2 \mid \langle f,\varphi\rangle \neq \infty\}.</math> The subspace <math>D(A)</math> contains all the <math>L^2</math> functions with compact support. Since <math>\mathbf{1}_{[-n,n]} \cdot \varphi\ \stackrel{L^2}{\to}\ \varphi,</math> <math>A</math> is densely defined. For every <math>\varphi \in D(A)</math> and <math>\psi \in D(A^*),</math>

:<math>\langle \varphi, A^*\psi \rangle = \langle A\varphi, \psi \rangle = \langle \langle f,\varphi \rangle\varphi_0, \psi \rangle = \langle f,\varphi \rangle\cdot \langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle = \langle \varphi, \langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle f\rangle. </math>

Thus, <math>A^* \psi = \langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle f.</math> The definition of adjoint operator requires that <math>\mathop{\text{Im}}A^* \subseteq H=L^2.</math> Since <math>f \notin L^2,</math> this is only possible if <math>\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle= 0.</math> For this reason, <math>D(A^*) = \{\varphi_0\}^\perp.</math> Hence, <math>A^*</math> is not densely defined and is identically zero on <math>D(A^*).</math> As a result, <math>A</math> is not closable and has no second adjoint <math>A^{**}.</math>

== Hermitian operators==
A [[bounded operator]] {{math|''A'' : ''H'' → ''H''}} is called Hermitian or [[Self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]] if
:<math>A = A^*</math>

which is equivalent to
:<math>\langle Ax , y \rangle = \langle x , A y \rangle \mbox{ for all } x, y \in H.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Reed|Simon|2003|pp=187}}; {{harvnb|Rudin|1991|loc=§12.11}}</ref>

In some sense, these operators play the role of the [[real number]]s (being equal to their own "complex conjugate") and form a real [[vector space]]. They serve as the model of real-valued [[observable]]s in [[quantum mechanics]]. See the article on [[self-adjoint operator]]s for a full treatment.

== Adjoints of conjugate-linear operators ==
For a [[Antilinear map|conjugate-linear operator]] the definition of adjoint needs to be adjusted in order to compensate for the complex conjugation. An adjoint operator of the conjugate-linear operator {{mvar|A}} on a complex Hilbert space {{mvar|H}} is an conjugate-linear operator {{math|''A''<sup>∗</sup> : ''H'' → ''H''}} with the property:

: <math>\langle Ax , y \rangle = \overline{\left\langle x , A^* y \right\rangle} \quad \text{for all } x, y \in H.</math>

== Other adjoints ==
The equation
: <math>\langle Ax , y \rangle = \left\langle x, A^* y \right\rangle</math>

is formally similar to the defining properties of pairs of [[adjoint functor]]s in [[category theory]], and this is where adjoint functors got their name.

The notion of adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces is also abstracted in the definition of a [[dagger category]] or [[dagger symmetric monoidal category]].
